Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The severe alert sent by the UK government on Friday warned of a ‘very high risk of wildfires’. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images Wildfires Alarmed by the alarm: people react to ‘severe alert’ on phones over UK wildfires Many complained online that piercingly loud tone was ‘overreach’ while others lamented lack of action on decarbonisation Sammy Gecsoyler Sat 15 Aug 2026 11.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 12.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On Friday at 7pm, Thérèse Coffey was nine miles away from a nuclear power station when her phone made a loud, piercing and very worrying sound: it was a “severe” emergency alert . “Was expecting [a] much more specific alert, not a generic message on wildfires,” the former Conservative cabinet minister said on X. She wasn’t alone in being alarmed by the alarm sent to phones in England and Wales. In the aftermath, thousands of social media users expressed their shock at alert. Some shared funny memes and others lamented what they viewed as lack of government action on decarbonisation. Academic John Ritzema called it a “massive overreach” and said the alert system should be “be for ‘drop everything and prepare for something terrible’ situations”, something Coffey echoed, saying alerts should not become commonplace to avoid “Peter cries wolf situations”. Even broadcasters were taken by surprise. The alert sounded live on the BBC’s The One Show, with host Ronan Kemp saying : “We’ve got some form of fire alarm going on.” Chris Packham used the alert to plug a parliamentary petition calling for a UK-wide briefing on climate and nature risks. The alert on Friday night came as Andy Burnham spent time in Stourbridge in the West Midlands earlier that day after homes were destroyed and residents were left injured by a series of fires. The prime minister warned that Britain “is a tinderbox right now”, with the public set for a “difficult weekend”. It has been a record year of wildfires in England and Wales: the number so far has passed the 1,017 recorded in 2025. Fire services declared 11 major incidents in a 24-hour period starting on Thursday. People have been urged not to light barbecues, campfires, fireworks or anything else that could spark a blaze while the wildfire risk remains high. They have also been urged to call 999 immediately if they spot a fire. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Hot topic: why is Burnham so reluctant to talk about the climate crisis? Read more The wildfires have also prompted calls within the Labour party to accelerate action against the climate crisis. Sadiq Khan warned Burnham not to “slow down on net zero” and said the heatwave and wildfires showed the need for action on climate change. The London mayor described the planet as being in a “deeply precarious position”. “We need reassurance from the government that they won’t slow down on net zero or reducing our reliance on oil and gas and that they’ll continue accelerating the green investment we need to get our country and planet back on track,” he said. Burnham announced a temporary national ban on the sale of disposable barbecues , to be enforced immediately. The ban will remain in place as long as the risk of wildfires remains high. The military was called in to assist stretched emergency services in south Wales . About 100 personnel were deployed, with about 100 more due to arrive on Friday evening, distributing water and providing logistical support. Burnham also announced £65m of extra ⁠funding for ⁠farmers ​hit by a drought. He said on X: “Today we’re putting £65m more into ⁠supporting farmers through this drought and preparing ​for the ‌summers ahead. They’re ‌on the frontline of a ‌changing climate and they shouldn’t be left to face it alone. “The ability to grow our own food is ‌national security. I’ll treat it that way,” he said. Britain’s cereal harvest ​is on track to be ​the ‌worst since comparable ​records ​began in 1984, according to an analysis published earlier this month. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: This week, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport. Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/AP View image in fullscreen This week, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport. Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/AP Germany Analysis Leipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over Russia Kate Connolly in Berlin The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left Wed 2 Sep 2026 13.07 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.12 EDT Share Even before the German government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport , the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda. But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue. Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow to Germany once again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine. Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours. An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high ‌alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure. Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions. Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure. The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”. While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. ( Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack , with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.) “This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”. The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions against Russia , and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking. Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke. Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion With the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure. Within Merz’s own party, there have been growing calls for him to toughen his stance against Moscow and pure frustration that it has taken so long. For years, members of his Christian Democrats and his current coalition partner, the Social Democrats, along with generations of diplomats, have remained caught up in, and seduced by, the long-standing romantic notion that Russia could be tamed by trade and energy pipelines, according to the CDU’s Roderich Kiesewetter. The former soldier and the party’s respected foreign policy expert told broadcaster InfoRadio that Germany “must give up its caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil, as well as this romantic notion of Russia as a great cultural nation. Russia cares not a damn about this caution, but rather sees it as an invitation to keep escalating.” He criticised Merz’s recent public reference to Russia as a great cultural nation, “because great cultural nations do not subject their neighbouring states to war, violence and child abductions”. He said it was time for Merz to name the current Russian regime for what it was. Konstantin von Notz, foreign policy expert for the Greens, praised the government’s “significantly clear language” over Moscow’s behaviour, even as he described it as “long overdue”. The extent to which voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear how a further deterioration of relations with Moscow could affect them may yet be felt at the ballot box. https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-20.text: Maariv pollster Dr. Menachem Lazar discussed the newspaper's latest election poll published Friday, highlighting the parties still struggling to secure enough support to enter the Knesset, Blue and White chairman and former defense minister Benny Gantz's weak showing among smaller parties, and challenges facing Likud and its allies.“There are currently two or three parties that are still in the danger zone: Am Yisrael on one side, which is passing the electoral threshold by fractions of a percentage point, and its counterpart, the Reservists and Economic Party, which is not passing the electoral threshold, also by fractions of a percentage point,” Lazar said.He added: “To them, we can add the Religious Zionism and Zehut list, which is passing the electoral threshold, but still cannot rest on its laurels.”Lazar noted that Gantz remains the only figure among the smaller lists to receive more than 1% support, but said he is still far from crossing the electoral threshold.“Among all the other lists that submitted themselves for election, it does not appear that any of them is currently succeeding in obtaining a significant number of votes,” he said.Lazar said the bloc of Zionist opposition parties has managed to stabilize itself ahead of the election.“The picture there is clear. There is also an even number of parties, so the surplus-vote agreements will prevent wasted votes,” he said.He said the merger of Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad has so far failed to live up to its potential, while Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, has maintained stability at five seats.Voter turnout among Arab citizensLazar also addressed voter turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, saying it could significantly affect the strength of Arab parties.“For now, it appears that voter turnout in Arab society is not increasing. The higher the voter turnout, the greater the power of the Arab parties will be,” he said. “Arab citizens of Israel make up about 21% of the country's population. If the voting rate in Arab society is similar to the voting rate in Jewish society, the Arab parties can reach 17 seats.”Lazar also said Likud's recent primaries and reserved slots did not give the party a significant boost.“The struggles within the bloc, between Likud and Otzma Yehudit, Religious Zionism, and Am Yisrael, are currently not benefiting Likud,” he said.Haredi parties face internal challenges“On the other hand, the bloc also has the haredi parties. United Torah Judaism, an exceptional party of political stability since 1992, has become an arena of internal conflict between its main groups, the hassidic and Lithuanian factions. Shas has so far failed to create new momentum and has continued to stagnate at seven seats for a long period.”Lazar estimated that voter uncertainty will continue to decline after the holiday, with more Israelis deciding which party they will support.“We can already see that the percentage of undecided voters is declining, and it will likely continue to decline,” he concluded.
